h: About the screens in this tutorial
x: A hands-on guide to the Robo Architect Lite desktop app, step by step from scratch: turn a one-line requirement into a proposal, break it down with domain-driven design (DDD), set a project constitution and a plan, have Claude Code implement it in a sandbox, then validate it against acceptance criteria and merge it back into the design. What Robo Architect is Robo Architect is a spec-driven development (SDD) tool . The spec, not the code, is the source of truth. You write requirements in plain language, and AI breaks them down into the vocabulary of domain-driven design (DDD) — bounded contexts, aggregates, commands, events, and acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then form. Claude Code writes the code from that design, and the finished code is checked against the design again. Every change is handled as one proposal . A proposal moves through these stages. Stage What happens In this tutorial INTENT Breaks a plain-language requirement into a strategic design (processes, bounded contexts, features, user stories, acceptance criteria) Chapter 3 PLAN Decides the tactical design, architecture and impact, based on the project constitution Chapters 4 · 5 IMPLEMENTING Claude Code implements it in a separate Git worktree (the sandbox) Chapter 6 VALIDATING · Pending Acceptance Runs structural validation and acceptance-criteria tests Chapter 7 ACCEPTED On acceptance, the code is merged into the main branch and written into the design graph Chapter 7 This tutorial uses Robo Architect Lite , a desktop app you use on your own computer. It stores the design not in Neo4j but in a graph in Ontological DB , one graph per project. There is no sign-in screen, and AI work is done by Claude Code on your computer. The story You will build Hanbit Delivery , a delivery service that connects neighborhood restaurants with customers. You play Jinyoung Jang , who is in charge of designing the service. Who Role Jinyoung Jang Hanbit Delivery's architect — the person you play in this tutorial Store owner Registers the store's menu items and accepts incoming orders Customer Picks menu items and orders, and can cancel before the store accepts Claude Code The AI teammate that follows skills to break down the design, make the plan and write the code Getting started — install the app, create your first project and tour the screens. The proposal lifecycle — turn the “register menu items and order” requirement into a proposal and get a strategic design, set the project constitution and make a plan, then implement in a sandbox, validate and accept. Design and change — view the accepted design in the Requirements, Process, Design and Data tabs, read how a second requirement affects the existing design in the Impact Map, and look inside the engine's skill files. Legacy and data — connect Hanbit Delivery's existing order DB as a data source, start a design from a requirements document, and analyze the old order system's code to design a new feature on the evidence of its business rules. Final project — add a review feature yourself, from start to finish. Learning path Getting started Installation and your first project, a tour of the screens The proposal lifecycle Create a proposal, constitution, plan, sandbox implementation, validation and acceptance Design and change Design tour, the change impact of a second proposal, changing the engine with skill files Legacy and data Connect data sources, start a design from a requirements document, analyze legacy code and design on its evidence Final project Capstone — a review feature Each chapter follows the order why → hands-on → quiz . Later chapters build on what you made in earlier ones, so it's best to follow them in order. The quiz answers are folded; try the questions yourself first, then expand them. Who this tutorial is for Developers who have built a web service at least once, or planners and architects who work with requirements and design. You don't need to know DDD. t: Install and create your first project
x: Install the Robo Architect Lite desktop app and launch it for the first time, check that it brings up the graph DB and analysis services in Docker, then create your first project, “hanbit_delivery_en”, on Home, choose its code folder and open it. What gets installed Lite runs as one desktop app and seven Docker containers. When you start the app, it brings up the containers itself; when you quit, it leaves them running (so the next start is faster). Component What it does Desktop app The screens, plus the Robo Architect backend running on your computer graph-db Ontological DB — stores the design as a graph. Each project gets its own graph graph-bolt The graph DB's Bolt-protocol entry point. The app sends its queries here fabric · catalog Connect data sources (existing DBs) to the graph DB and organize their schemas (Chapter 11) analyzer · parser · gateway Read and analyze legacy code Neo4j is not used. Earlier versions of Robo Architect kept the design in Neo4j, but Lite uses Ontological DB, where the graph DB itself also connects to your data sources. Prerequisites Item Details Docker Desktop Install it and keep it running . 20 GB of free disk space and 16 GB of memory or more are recommended Claude Code Run claude once in a terminal and sign in. Proposal analysis, planning and implementation all run through it Git git --version should print a version OpenAI API key Used only for document upload in the Requirements tab. You can follow this whole tutorial (Chapters 3–14) without a key — legacy code analysis (Chapter 13) also runs through Claude Code What Claude Code does Robo Architect's engine is not a built-in AI pipeline but Claude Code skills . When you create a proposal, the app calls claude on your computer and has it do the work by following a skill file (Chapter 10). That's why you don't need to enter a separate API key, and why you can also use the same skills directly from Claude Code in a terminal. Hands-on 1 — Install Download the installer for macOS (Apple silicon) or Windows (x64) from GitHub Releases . macOS (Apple silicon) Download Robo-Architect-Lite-mac-arm64.dmg , open it and drag Robo Architect Lite to Applications . It is for M1 or later Macs (to check your chip: 🍎 menu → About This Mac). All installer files are on GitHub Releases . Open the app. When macOS says it “could not verify ‘Robo Architect Lite’ is free of malware”, click Done , open System Settings › Privacy & Security , click Open Anyway next to Robo Architect Lite and enter your password. Click Open in the dialog that follows. The build is not notarized by Apple yet, so this is needed only the first time (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open ). On first launch the app downloads the seven container images (about 1.1 GB to download, about 4.8 GB on disk) from the GitHub Container Registry ( ghcr.io/uengine-oss/robo-architect-lite-* ). Home shows which image is downloading and how far it is. Later launches skip the download. Windows For Windows 10/11 (x64). Keep Docker Desktop running on its default WSL 2 backend (Linux containers) , and install Git for Windows as well — Claude Code needs it. Download Robo-Architect-Lite-Setup-win-x64.exe (about 190 MB) and run it. When “Windows protected your PC” appears, click More info , then Run anyway . The build is not code-signed yet, so this appears the first time. Choose where to install and finish (over 20,000 files, so it takes a few minutes). Leave the install scope at its default (the current user) and you don't need administrator rights. Uncheck the “Run” option on the last screen — an app launched from the installer inherits the environment the installer started with. Open the app from the Start menu. On first launch the app downloads the seven container images (about 1.1 GB) from the GitHub Container Registry, as on macOS. Later launches skip the download. t: Create a proposal — from one requirement to strategic design
x: Write “store owners register menu items; customers pick items, order, and can cancel before the store accepts” in plain language to create your first proposal, then read the strategic design Claude Code splits it into (processes · bounded contexts · features · user stories · acceptance criteria) and the Impact Map. Why a proposal In Robo Architect you don't change code directly. When you want to change something, you first create a proposal . One proposal is one change, and it keeps the whole history, from “what are we changing and why” (strategic design) to “how did we build it, and did we build it right” (implementation and validation). So when someone later asks “why does this aggregate exist?”, you open that proposal. The first stage of a proposal is INTENT . It splits the requirement sentence into the vocabulary of domain-driven design (DDD). What you get Meaning Process The order in which the work flows. e.g. register menu item → change price → mark sold out Bounded context An area in which the same word always means the same thing. Classified as Core · Supporting · Generic Feature A group of functions inside a context User story “Who · what · why” Acceptance criteria Given (in this situation) · When (you do this) · Then (this happens). They later become tests as they are (Chapter 7) Hands-on 1 — Create a proposal On Home, click the Proposals card to open the Proposals tab. Click + New Proposal at the top right. Type the requirement into the input box. Leave the mode at Simplified (Intent → Plan). Detailed DDD confirms the DDD stages Discover → Decompose → … → Tactical one by one, and ODA Standard designs on the basis of the TM Forum ODA standards. Click Start AI Analysis . New Proposal — the requirement input box and Simplified · Detailed DDD · ODA Standard The analysis is done by Claude Code on your computer, following the robo-proposal-intent skill. The progress window streams the tools Claude uses and its reasoning as they happen. It's normal for every legacy graph search ( cluster_retrieve ) to end with “0 legacy candidates · 0 rules found” — no existing code has been analyzed yet (once you analyze existing code in Chapter 13, evidence shows up here). One of the searches may be a Korean rewording of the requirement: the skill instructions are written in Korean, so Claude also tries Korean keywords in case the existing code uses them. Decomposing the natural-language intent — Claude Code's tool calls and the legacy graph search log In this tutorial, “Proposal PRO-001 draft has been created.” appeared after about 2 minutes (127 seconds), without any clarification questions. Click View Proposal . If the AI asks questions If the requirement is ambiguous, “AI would like to clarify a few things” appears during the analysis with some options. Pick an option or type your own answer and click Submit Answers ; to skip, click Continue with current info . The title is taken from a representative user story (“Store owner: register a menu item”), and the status is INTENT . h: Hands-on 1 — Create the constitution by interview
x: Before planning, decide this project's design principles · tech stack · architecture style · repository strategy once. Claude Code reads the proposal and offers questions and recommendations, you just pick the answers, and those answers become the constitution document. Why a constitution The same “Order” aggregate leads to completely different plans depending on whether you build it with Spring Boot or Node.js, and whether you split it into services or keep one. If you make those decisions again for every proposal, proposals end up building different structures. The constitution is the document where you write such decisions down once for the project. From then on, every proposal's plan (Chapter 5) and implementation (Chapter 6) follow the constitution, and each plan decision shows which passage of the constitution it came from. The constitution is a single Markdown document. Each section (##) holds declarations only. Section What it holds Core Principles Design principles, with a strength such as must (MUST) or cannot be changed (NON-NEGOTIABLE), and a rationale Technology Constraints Languages, frameworks, datastores Architecture Monolith/microservices, modules and dependency direction, layers Repository Strategy Monorepo/multi-repo, folder layout Governance Amendment procedure and versioning policy Hands-on 1 — Create the constitution by interview If you try to make a proposal's plan in a project without a constitution, “Constitution Required” appears and an interview opens. In the Proposals tab, open PRO-001 , click Proceed to Plan → at the bottom, then Generate Plan in the Plan section. The Project Constitution dialog opens, and Claude Code first analyzes this proposal (“[analysis] proposal PRO-001 — 2 BoundedContexts: Menu Management, Ordering”). Questions appear one at a time. The Rationale under a question is Claude Code's reason for its recommendation. Pick an option or type your own, then click Next question → . On the last question, click ✓ Create constitution . The constitution is saved, and plan generation continues automatically (Chapter 5). Question 1 — architecture style, Claude Code's rationale, and MONOLITH · Recommended / MICROSERVICES In this tutorial there were two questions. Question Rationale (reason for the recommendation) Answer chosen Architecture style Only 2 bounded contexts, both mostly CRUD, joined at one point (Ordering reads a menu item's price and sold-out status) — a modular monolith keeps them separate without the cost of distributed services MONOLITH (recommended) Tech stack (backend / frontend / datastore) The requirement names no technology, so this is a suggested default: the order-state rule and the checkout checks need ACID transactions (PostgreSQL), and Spring Boot's module support can keep the two contexts apart in one deployable Typed in: Backend TypeScript (Node.js, Express) / Frontend React / Datastore SQLite Question 2 — tech stack: three options (Spring Boot + JPA + PostgreSQL + Vue 3 …) and a free-text field holding Claude Code's suggestion, Java 21 + Spring Boot 3 You don't have to follow the recommendation The recommended tech stack was Spring Boot (Java 21 + Spring Boot 3, typed into the field for you), but this tutorial replaced it with Node.js and SQLite to get the implementation running quickly. The constitution records your answers as “confirmed by the user in the interview”. The number of questions and their options depend on the proposal. Hands-on 2 — Read the constitution You can open the constitution at any time from the Project Constitution card on Home (or the Constitution button in the Design tab's navigator). Project Constitution — Preview · Edit, “Set up by interview”, Hanbit Delivery Constitution You answered only two questions, but Claude Code read the proposal's strategic design and set out seven principles. The ones it added on its own, beyond your requirement and answers, are marked (recommended) . Principle Gist I. Bounded Contexts as Modules Two modules,

Based on the constitution, Claude Code sets the proposal's tactical design (aggregates · commands · events · read models) and its architecture decisions (deployment · data access · API contracts · authentication · test strategy). Each decision cites the constitution passage it rests on, and areas the constitution is silent on surface as a “Constitution Gap”. Why a plan The strategic design (Chapter 3) is the “what”. To implement it, you need the “how”. The plan decides two things. Tactical design — the building blocks of DDD: aggregates (the unit that keeps consistency), commands (requests that change state), events (facts that happened) and read models (models for queries) Architecture decisions — things like deployment units, data access, API contracts, authentication and test strategy. Each decision states which passage of the constitution it came from Hands-on 1 — Generate the plan In the Plan section of PRO-001 , click Generate Plan (if you just created the constitution, it starts by itself). “Claude is drafting the tactical breakdown and architecture plan…” and the elapsed time appear. It usually takes 5–12 minutes; in this tutorial it took about 11½ minutes (693 seconds, counted from the moment the constitution was saved). Generating the plan — elapsed time, “Usually takes 5–12 minutes”, and the warning that reloading or moving to another screen starts over Stay on that screen while it generates Plan generation works by having the screen receive the result as it streams, so reloading during generation, or moving to another screen in that tab, starts it over from the beginning. If you want to do something else, open a new tab from Home. Hands-on 2 — Read the plan When generation finishes, the progress log is at the top, followed by Architecture Decisions (Constitution-based) , Constitution Gap , Tactical Design , and a summary. Plan result — the progress log (one “tactical” line per element) and the start of the architecture decisions Architecture decisions Each decision shows, next to its title, the constitution sections it rests on (e.g. ↳ Architecture (Deployment environment); VII. Simplicity; Technology Constraints (Datastore) ). This time there were eleven decisions; here are some of them. Decision Content Based on Deployment Env One Node.js LTS process runs Express; it serves the REST API under /api and the built React assets, packaged as one container image with one SQLite file on a persistent volume Architecture, VII, Technology Constraints Ingress · Service Mesh / Framework N/A, it's a monolith. Express with TypeScript strict mode; each module is layered domain → application → infrastructure → interface, and Ordering calls only Menu Management's published MenuCatalogQuery port ( OrderableMenuItems ), in-process Architecture, I, Technology Constraints Repo Mapping Monorepo with npm workspaces: backend/src/modules/menu-management , backend/src/modules/ordering , backend/migrations , frontend/ Repository Strategy LIBRARIES (data access, tests) better-sqlite3 with hand-written SQL (no ORM); state-changing commands run in BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions that re-check the state, so a conflicting AcceptOrder and CancelOrder can't both succeed; Vitest (test-first) · Supertest · React Testing Library Technology Constraints, VI API_ERROR_MAPPING Domain errors map to explicit 4xx: invalid input 400, not your store or order 403, sold out · different store · items changed · illegal transition 409, unknown 404 Technology Constraints (API style) AUTHENTICATION A middleware resolves ActorContext {actorId, role, ownedStoreIds} and the services check role and ownership; how users log in and who owns which store is left open, with a development stub for now none — marked Constitution Gap (see below) Architecture decisions — Deployment Env · Ingress · Service Mesh / Framework, each with the constitution sections it rests on Constitution Gap Areas the plan needs but the constitution doesn't decide appear in a yellow box. When implementation is finished, “Done → Verify” checks the sandbox code against the design. Structural validation (robo-sync: are the design's aggregates · commands · events in the code?) and acceptance criteria (do the Given · When · Then hold?) are reviewed together, and if they pass, “Accept (Dual Merge)” merges the code and the design graph into the main line at once. In this tutorial all 52 checks passed, with 0 failures and 0 SKIPs, and validation through acceptance took about 8 minutes. Why validate The AI ticking every item on the task list is no guarantee that the code was built as designed. Validation looks at two things. Structural validation — whether the tactical design's (Chapter 5) aggregates · fields · commands · events are in the code. The robo-sync extractor pulls them out of the code and matches them against the design. Acceptance criteria — for each Given · When · Then in the strategic design (Chapter 3), it reads the code and tests to judge whether it holds, and attaches evidence (the code that enforces it, the tests that passed). Hands-on 1 — Run validation When the progress bar reaches 18/18, Done → Verify appears in the Sandbox Implementation section. Click it. You move to the Validation section and the log streams (“Loaded 24 acceptance criteria + structural targets. Comparing with the robo-sync extractor…”). To stop midway, click Stop . In this tutorial, the results came out after about 7½ minutes . Validation result — Total 52 · PASS 52 · FAIL 0 · SKIP 0, pass rate 100%, then the first card, SC-001 RegisterMenuItem (opened again after acceptance, so the badge already reads ACCEPTED) Hands-on 2 — Read the results Kind Count PASS FAIL SKIP Acceptance criteria 24 24 0 0 Structural validation 28 28 0 0 Total 52 52 0 0 The 28 structural checks are the tactical design's elements: 3 aggregates, 10 commands, 10 events and 5 read models. The pass rate is PASS ÷ Total = 52 ÷ 52 = 100% . Each card shows the verdict, the kind (Acceptance · Structural), the target (e.g. RegisterMenuItem ), the scenario number ( SC-001 ) and the evidence. For example, SC-002 says “registering a menu item with an empty name or a price of 0 or less returns InvalidMenuItemError and adds nothing”. Its evidence is that the MenuItem aggregate's register() collects the violations (blank name, price not a whole number above 0) and throws InvalidMenuItemError (400) before anything is saved, and that the throw rolls back the transaction. Acceptance criteria cards — SC-002 and SC-003 for RegisterMenuItem and SC-004 for ChangeMenuItemPrice, each with its scenario and evidence What SKIP means There were no SKIPs this time. A SKIP means a check couldn't be judged automatically; it isn't a failure. The usual cause is a command with no type of its own: if a command exists only as service method arguments and a zod schema, the extractor can't pull out its input fields. The validator may read the code and note “the inputs match the spec”, but since that isn't an automatic match, it records SKIP rather than PASS. In this run every command had its own input type, such as ChangeMenuItemPriceCommand { menuItemId, price } , so all 10 commands were matched field by field. (The extractor reads only the first exported class in a file, so the validator ran it on copies of each declaration — command inputs, event payloads, value objects — to compare them all.) To keep SKIPs at zero Keep commands as types, as in this run ( RegisterMenuItemCommand , ChangeMenuItemPriceCommand , …), so the extractor can read them. If you want this as a team rule, write it into the constitution (Chapter 4) or the implementation skill (Chapter 10). Hands-on 3 — Accept (Dual Merge) Open the Accept / Destroy section. Under “PO Final Decision” there are ✓ Accept (Dual Merge) and ✗ Destroy . If there are failures (FAIL), you must tick “I acknowledge the failures and will proceed with Accept” before Accept can be clicked. There were no failures this time, so it was enabled right away

x: Every instruction Robo Architect follows when it analyzes, plans and implements a proposal is written as text in a skill file (SKILL.md). Skills are the engine Every time Chapters 3–5 said “Claude Code analyzes”, the app called claude on your computer and handed it one skill file as its instructions. A skill file is a Markdown document — purpose, procedure, output format and rules, written as text a person can read. Change this text, without touching any code, and the engine's judgment changes. Stage Skill In this tutorial INTENT — strategic design robo-proposal-intent Chapter 3 Constitution — recommendations and the document robo-project-constitution Chapter 4 PLAN — tactical design · architecture robo-proposal-plan Chapter 5 Task list robo-proposal-tasks Chapter 6 Implementation — /robo-implement PRO-001 in the Code tab's cell robo-implement Chapter 6 Validation robo-proposal-test · robo-sync Chapter 7 Impact analysis robo-proposal-context Chapter 9 Detailed DDD stages robo-proposal-discover · -decompose · -strategize · -connect · -define · -scope · -tactical “Detailed DDD” in Chapter 3 The skills live in three bundle folders — robo-proposals/ (proposal stages), robo-spec/ (implementation · reverse sync) and robo-changes/ (requirement changes). h: Hands-on 5 — Design a new feature from legacy evidence
x: Analyze the old order system (Java · DDL) that Hanbit Delivery uses today into a code graph and a data schema, then design a new feature, “order rejection reasons”, as a proposal grounded in that graph. Claude Code on your computer does both the analysis and the design, so no OpenAI key is needed. Designing from an old system So far you've designed by putting requirements into an empty project. Real work is usually changing or rebuilding a system that's already running . The most expensive mistake then is to design the new one without knowing the business rules the old system already enforces. Rules like “only orders waiting for acceptance can be rejected” or “closing the store rejects all waiting orders at once” aren't in any document. They're only in the code. This chapter has two parts. Part What it does Result 1. Analysis Analyze the old code folder in Legacy › Code Code graph (classes · methods · business rules · examples) · data schema (tables · column descriptions) 2. Design from evidence Put a new requirement into a proposal, and the INTENT skill searches the analysis graph and attaches evidence to each element “Evidence n/m”, evidence tags · source code for each element The practice code Download hanbit-legacy.zip and unzip it (it unzips into a hanbit-legacy folder). It's the old order system Hanbit Delivery has used since 2016: Java 8 + JDBC, with the PostgreSQL schema delivery you connected in Chapter 11 as its DB. File What it does schema/delivery.sql 7 tables (customer · store · menu · orders · order_item · rider · delivery) order/OrderService.java Place · accept · reject · start cooking · cancel an order. The store's status changes (accept · reject · start cooking) all go through one changeStatus store/StoreService.java Open the store · close the store (rejects all waiting orders) menu/MenuService.java · delivery/DeliveryService.java · report/SettlementReport.java Menus · delivery · daily settlement Order status goes WAITING → ACCEPTED → COOKING → DELIVERING → DELIVERED , and can end as CANCELLED or REJECTED along the way. When an order is rejected, the reason isn't stored anywhere . That's what you'll fix in Part 2. Common sticking points in installation · projects · proposals · Claude Code · data sources, and how to get past them. Installing and running Do I need to install Neo4j separately? No. Lite keeps the design in Ontological DB. The app itself brings up the seven containers for the graph DB and analysis services in Docker (Chapter 1). Do I need an OpenAI API key? Not for this tutorial. Proposal analysis · planning · implementation are done by Claude Code on your computer, and a requirements document is also split without a key if you paste it into a proposal (Chapter 12). Legacy code analysis (Chapter 13) works without one too — the app hands the analyzer's AI calls to Claude Code. An OpenAI key is needed only for in-app AI helpers such as document upload in the Requirements tab and chat edits in the Design tab. Why is Claude Code needed? Because Robo Architect's engine is Claude Code's skills. Run claude once in a terminal and sign in, and the app calls the skills with that sign-in (Chapter 10). Projects Can I create several projects? Yes. In Switch project on Home, type a new name and click Create , and another graph is created. Each project has its own graph, so designs never mix. skill_lab_en in Chapter 10 is an example. My project name is rejected. It must start with a lowercase letter, use only lowercase letters · digits · underscores (_), and be 2–40 characters long. hanbit-delivery (hyphen) or Hanbit (uppercase) won't work. Proposals Plan generation started over from the beginning. If you reload that tab or move to another screen in it during generation, it starts over. While you wait, open a new tab from Home for other work. I get “Failed to parse the task breakdown”. It means the response from Claude during task list generation couldn't be read as a task list. Click Generate task list again. In this tutorial the first attempt worked and produced 18 tasks. After I changed the constitution, the plan became “stale”. That plan relied on the constitution. Regenerate the plan of that proposal and confirm it (Chapter 4). I want to change the constitution interview's questions. The order of questions is decided by the app. The robo-project-constitution skill handles the questions' recommendations · rationales and the constitution document (Chapter 10). Claude Code The terminal in the Code tab asks for a text color theme first. Claude Code asks once, the first time it runs in a terminal on this computer. Choose with the up and down arrows and press Enter. When I start implementation, “Is this a project you created or one you trust?” appears. It's the folder trust check Claude Code shows the first time it opens the sandbox folder. The default choice is “No, exit”, so press the down arrow to select Yes, I trust this folder and press Enter. When the bypass-permissions consent appears next, choose Yes, I accept . If implementation didn't start, type /robo-implement PRO-001 into the cell yourself. Data sources The connection test fails. If you put localhost in Host, change it to host.docker.internal . The side testing the connection is the data fabric inside a container, and localhost inside it is the container itself (Chapter 11).
